text: Every pipeline eventually needs data that doesn't live in a file you already have — it lives behind an API. This lesson uses GitHub's real, public REST API, no toy example, no authentication needed for read-only requests against public repositories.

requests.get sends the HTTP request and hands you back a Response object. .json parses the response body — which is just a JSON string, exactly like json.loads from two lessons ago — into a Python dict. Status 200 means it worked, and every field you're reading back, like stargazers_count, is real, live data that changes every day.

Here's the trap: a typo'd URL doesn't raise a Python exception on its own. GitHub just hands back a 404 with a perfectly normal, well-formed JSON body. Code that calls .json and reaches straight into data full_name without checking the status first crashes with a confusing KeyError — not an error that actually tells you what went wrong.

raise_for_status is the cleaner alternative to checking status codes by hand — it raises requests.HTTPError on any 4xx or 5xx response. Wrap that in the try/except pattern from last lesson and you've got something you'll reuse constantly once you're pulling data from APIs in real ETL pipelines.

Not every endpoint hands back one object — the contributors endpoint returns a JSON array instead, where each item is a dict with keys like login and contributions. By default GitHub only returns the first 30 contributors per page, which is exactly the limitation you'll fix next lesson.
Next up: pagination and rate limits. You'll learn to walk through every page of a result automatically, and respect the real ceiling GitHub puts on how many requests you can make per hour.
